title: Joe Russo's modern pit band at the Orpheum; Gallodoro's practice
summary: Weinstein describes Emil Tasso Sr.'s 27-year pit job ending and Joe Russo building a modern band with Gallodoro, who bought and practiced every clarinet. Jack and Howard were the brass team.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Now let's get back to Galadora. I would practice like mad. And during the time we were playing in the quarter, the Orphan Theatre had, for 27 years, had used the old-fashioned Pitt-type band, you know, only to play vortical. And Emil Tasso, Sr., had the job for 27 years. That's where that famous remark came from, was when he came home and told his wife, I got my notice, she said, I told you it wouldn't be a steady job. You've heard that before too. That's an epic down here. But they finally gave him his notice, and a young violinist by the name of Russo, Joseph Russo, or Joe Russo, was made the contractor, the leader actually, because in those days, they actually directed the Pitt. And he put a new type band in there. He got Howard Voorhees on trumpet and Al Galladora on saxophone, Henry Raymond on clarinet, on tenor saxophone. He had a modern type outfit. Instead of just Mr. Jufri on clarinet alone, and a flute player by the name of Jim Seger and so forth, they went into a more modern outfit. And Al got so bored playing fordable, you know, playing four shows a day, seven days a week, and you read the same music until at the end of the third show, you're not reading, you're just doing it by memory. He bought every clarinet and every saxophone. In those days, they had an F saxophone in between the E flat and the B flat. He bought an A clarinet, he bought a C clarinet, he bought a bass clarinet. And he'd go downstairs and practice each of them. And then he'd take, for instance, the A clarinet into the pit and read the B flat clarinet parts, which is a difficult transposition, half tone one way or the other, just so he could get to practice in odd keys. And as I say, when this guy, when you'd play with him, he would just sit there in astonishment, his fingers were like snakes. I've never ceased to admire this young man. But those were the days of transition because they did the same thing over at the Lowest State Theater and all these things died naturally. But these were all guys who came really from the field of dance music.
Where was Jack Asano playing? He played at the Orphan.

That's Jack. Yeah. It was the same group. I had forgotten to mention, but he and Howard were the brass team. Oh, and young Howard Reed was the second trumpet in the Orphan Theater pit. These were all young guys. I'm trying to remember who was on, I think it was Frank Cuny who played piano. And Russo on fiddle. And the bass player I think was one of the Brookhovans. I'm not too sure about that.
